I'm sure you have all heard of ChatGPT by now. It has become a buzzword within days of its release and professionals in all fields, especially in high skilled areas like lawyers, doctors, engineers are questioning whether such AI can actually replace them and work.

So in this video I want to talk about what ChatGPT is and how it even popped up, talk a bit about the organization behind GPT called "OpenAI", which has already created many other machine learning models besides Chat GPT and also explain technically about all that.
And then we'll dive in and actually put ChatGPT to use for some DevOps related tasks.
I really want to see how it can help in generating configuration code for building DevOps processes or different parts of those processes and how well it knows different DevOps technologies, but not just some shallow examples or boilerplate code that I can get from official documentation, but instead also try more fine-tuning and small optimizations in that configuration code.

We're also going to check out an open source command line tool that is built on top of ChatGPT and was specifically created for engineers to generate infrastructure as code templates and more and finally we'll talk about the impact of ChatGPT, the quality and usefulness of such a tool for engineers and whether it will really replace the engineers and to what extent you should be concerned.

Edureka’s DevOps online training is designed to help you master key tools of Devops lifecycle like Docker, Puppet, Jenkins, Nagios, GIT, Ansible, SaltStack and Chef used by a DevOps Engineer for automating multiple steps in SDLC. During this course, our expert DevOps instructors will help you:

videoTitle: The ONLY Roadmap to Get a DevOps Job in 2026 | Zero to Hero Guidance | Senior DevOps Engineer | USA
videoDescription:
This is the exact roadmap that will get you hired in 2026. 🚀

Stop following random roadmaps that leave you more confused than when you started. The DevOps landscape is shifting, and simply knowing a few tools isn't enough anymore. To land a high-paying role today, you need to understand the logic, the architecture, and the "why" behind every deployment.

I’m Avi (Vamsi Avinash Gunji). I’ve spent years navigating the enterprise tech world—from my first role at Clarivate in 2019 to roles at Farmers Insurance, The Home Depot, PwC, and Goldman Sachs, leading up to my current position as a Senior DevOps Engineer. I’ve seen what actually works in production and what’s just "tutorial noise."

In this video, I’m breaking down the definitive path I would follow if I were starting from zero today. We’re debugging your career "Desi style"—from code errors to chai breaks. This is my narrative—unfiltered, evolving, and unfinished.

📍 The Roadmap Breakdown:
In this video, we cover the critical phases to master:
✅ Phase 1: Mastering the Linux terminal, systemctl, and Bash/Python automation.
✅ Phase 1.2: Why Networking (DNS/VPCs) and Storage (NFS) are your best friends.
✅ Phase 2: Cloud architecture (AWS/Azure/GCP) vs. the reality of Private Cloud and On-Prem.
✅ Phase 3: Infrastructure as Code (Terraform & Ansible) to save you from disasters.
✅ Phase 4: Containers & Kubernetes (K8s)—The core of modern engineering.
✅ Phase 4.2: Building actual end-to-end CI/CD pipelines with Jenkins and GitHub Actions.
✅ Phase 5: Monitoring, Alerting, and Observability (Prometheus, Grafana, Splunk).

videoTitle: Cloud Engineer vs DevOps Engineer - Differences and Overlaps of tasks and responsibilities
videoDescription:
Differences and Overlaps of Cloud and DevOps Engineer Roles as well as deep dive of Cloud Engineer Tasks and Responsibilities

DevOps engineer and Cloud engineer are 2 popular roles in software engineering. But there is a lot of mix up of these two roles and many people and many companies often use them interchangeably. videoDescription:

Also how to approach implementing an IDP - internal developer platform.

In this video we're going to talk about a relatively new hot topic in DevOps and Cloud space, which is “platform engineering”. There is a lot of discussion going on, where some people are asking whether platform engineering replaces DevOps. Many people say it goes hand in hand and is rather an addition to DevOps, but in reality it's a bit more complicated than that. Platform engineering actually changes a lot of established rules we knew about DevOps, SRE and Cloud engineering, it changes the game and introduces some new rules.

So let's clearly define, what platform engineering exactly is, more interestingly, why was there even a need for this new role and how it evolved and of course how it compares to DevOps and Cloud engineering and does it really replace any of these roles?

videoTitle: 보이지 않는 다리, DevOps: 개발과 운영을 잇는 IT 세상의 숨고르기
videoDescription:
여러분은 하루 중 언제 쉬시나요?
저는 퇴근길 지하철에서 다리를 건너며 노을을 바라볼 때, 잠시 숨을 고릅니다.
IT 세계에도 이런 보이지 않는 다리가 있습니다. 바로 DevOps입니다.

DevOps는 Development(개발)과 Operations(운영)을 하나로 잇는 문화와 방법론입니다.
개발자가 새로운 기능을 만들고, 운영팀이 서버를 관리하던 과거에는 늘 벽이 있었습니다.
하지만 DevOps는 이 벽을 허물어, 서비스가 더 빠르고 안정적으로 배포되도록 합니다.

✨ DevOps 핵심 개념

자동화: 코드 작성 → 빌드 → 테스트 → 배포까지 자동 처리

CI/CD: 작은 기능도 자주, 안정적으로 배포

모니터링과 피드백: 실시간으로 문제 감지 & 개선

도구 활용: Jenkins, GitHub Actions, Docker, Kubernetes, Prometheus, Grafana

이제 DevOps는 클라우드와 만나 더 강력해졌습니다.
코드 한 줄 수정이 전 세계에 즉시 반영되는 CI/CD 파이프라인.
서버리스, API 게이트웨이, 컨테이너를 통한 마이크로서비스 아키텍처.
그리고 AI와 결합해 데이터 처리, 보안, 모델 최적화까지 개발자가 직접 다루는 시대가 되었습니다.

카카오톡이 멈추지 않고, 넷플릭스가 전 세계 수억 명에게 끊김 없이 영상을 제공할 수 있는 이유.
그 중심에는 항상 DevOps와 클라우드가 있습니다.

눈에 잘 띄지 않지만, 없으면 모든 게 멈추는 다리.
그게 바로 DevOps입니다.

오늘 영상이 도움이 되셨다면,
구독과 좋아요, 알림 설정으로 함께해주세요 🙌

videoTitle: InFocus - Honeycomb: Post-Merge Control #LaunchDarkly #FeatureFlags #DevOps
videoDescription:
After a merger, things can get messy fast.

For us, LaunchDarkly became the way to get control back, especially once real customers were on the line.

It’s not about hoping changes work. It’s about knowing you can flip a switch, roll things back, and stay in control when production gets unpredictable.
channelDescription:
LaunchDarkly is the runtime control layer for the AI era. For over a decade we have helped engineering teams control what ships in production, from feature flags to full release governance. Today that mission extends to the AI agents and code that are increasingly building, modifying, and operating software on behalf of engineering teams.

With CodeControl and AgentControl, teams can ship faster, govern what runs in production, and automatically respond when something needs to change, without waiting on a redeploy. LaunchDarkly runs on infrastructure that handles over 50 trillion flag evaluations a day, which means the same platform that governs your features also governs your agents.

Founded in 2014 by Edith Harbaugh and John Kodumal, LaunchDarkly has been named on the Forbes Cloud 100 list and serves some of the most demanding engineering teams in the world.

Learn more at launchdarkly.com

videoTitle: BTAIH E03 · Mohamed Daoudi, DevOps Engineer · Can AI Replace DevOps Engineers?
videoDescription:
My third guest on BTAIH is Mohamed Daoudi, a DevOps engineer whose path took him from ENSA and self-taught Linux and Docker to early-stage companies, large-scale cloud systems at Oracle, and independent consulting.

We get into what happens when AI stops being a chatbot and starts touching real infrastructure: writing scripts, handling repetitive migrations, executing commands, configuring CI/CD, connecting hosting and domains, and helping ship a working website in less than 24 hours.

It is a practical conversation, not a hype one. Where AI genuinely makes a DevOps engineer faster, where it turns 100 lines into 10,000, and why giving an agent access to your systems is only useful when you still understand the infrastructure underneath it.

About Mohamed

Mohamed Daoudi is a DevOps engineer with experience across startups, service companies, Oracle Cloud and independent consulting. His work has included CI/CD, Kubernetes, cloud infrastructure, incident management and keeping production systems stable at scale.

Find Mohamed

LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/iduoad/
X: https://x.com/MIduoad

About the show

Beyond The AI Hype (BTAIH) is a podcast about AI, engineering, and building a tech career, hosted by Abderrahman Jaize. We talk in Darija, English, and French, usually all three in the same sentence.

Chapters

كيف يؤثر الذكاء الاصطناعي على حياتنا اليومية؟ تعرف على المهارات التقنية الأساسية التي تحتاجها للبقاء في سوق العمل خلال العصر الرقمي القادم.

يقدم هذا المقطع نظرة شاملة حول الكيفية التي يعيد بها الذكاء الاصطناعي صياغة واقعنا المعاصر. إذا كنت ترغب في فهم التغيرات الجذرية التي تنتظرنا، فإننا نستعرض هنا كيف أصبحت الأنظمة البرمجية هي المحرك الأساسي للاقتصاد والمجتمع في هذا العصر الرقمي.

سيتعلم المشاهدون أهمية امتلاك المهارات التقنية اللازمة لمواكبة التطورات المستمرة. نناقش بالتفصيل لماذا لم يعد الإلمام بالتقنية خياراً، بل ضرورة حتمية للنجاح المهني والشخصي، حيث يمتد تأثير الذكاء الاصطناعي ليطال كل تفاصيل حياتنا، مما يجعل فهم الأنظمة البرمجية مهارة لا غنى عنها.

اشترك في القناة للحصول على تحليلات أسبوعية حول مستقبل التكنولوجيا، وأخبرنا في التعليقات: ما هو المجال الذي تعتقد أن الذكاء الاصطناعي سيغيره بشكل أكبر في السنوات القادمة؟

videoTitle: Guided DevOps Meditation
videoDescription:
Dive into a unique meditative experience designed specifically for the DevOps Engineer. In the hustle of ensuring seamless deployments and system operations, every DevOps professional deserves a moment to reboot, refresh, and recenter.

Whether you're in the midst of a complex project or wrapping up a day of successful deployments, this meditation will guide you to find serenity amidst the codes and systems.

🔗 Find tranquility amidst the binaries. Hit play and embark on a journey to the calm side of DevOps.

Don't forget to LIKE, SHARE, and SUBSCRIBE for more content dedicated to the DevOps community! 🚀👍

▬▬▬▬▬▬ S C R I P T  📜  ▬▬▬▬▬▬

"Begin by finding a serene place where you can sit undisturbed. As you prepare to delve into a state of calm, think of it as setting up the perfect environment for a seamless deployment."

"Sit or lie down in a comfortable position, ensuring that your back is straight and your hands rest lightly on your lap or by your sides. Close your eyes gently. Let's begin our system reboot."

"Start by taking a deep breath in, inhaling calmness and clarity, like the smooth initiation of a well-planned product. And exhale, releasing any system glitches or unwanted bugs from your mind."

"Imagine your mind as a server room. Each server represents a thought or a responsibility in your life. Some servers are humming busily, while others are quiet and in standby mode."

"Visualize a cooling system, a gust of fresh, clean air entering the room, stabilizing the temperature. This cooling breath ensures that every server, every thought, operates at its peak without overheating."

"As you continue breathing deeply, bring to mind a continuous integration and continuous deployment pipeline. With every inhale, new features and positive affirmations are integrated. With every exhale, new code is deployed to production."

"Imagine a monitoring dashboard, showcasing green status indicators. Your body is this system. Your heart rate, your breathing, your state of calm are all in optimal state - all systems operational and running smoothly."

"Think about the code commits. Sometimes, errors occur, and that's okay. Acknowledge them without judgment, fix them, and move on. For now, release any attachment to those errors, letting them float away like logs being archived."

"Your breathing is now your main server, your central command. Focus on its rhythm, the gentle in-and-out, the same predictable yet vital process, akin to the regular checks and balances in DevOps."

"Even in the face of challenges, remember that every system has its recovery procedure. Your mind, your spirit, and your body are no different. You have the resilience, the backup plans, and the capability for recovery."

"Slowly begin to transition, like smoothly moving from development to production. Become aware of your surroundings. Feel the chair or the floor supporting you, the gentle rhythm of your heart."

"When you're ready, with the confidence of a successful code deployment, open your eyes. As you go back into the world, remember that just like in DevOps, balance, continuous improvement, and adaptation are key."

videoTitle: 😱Hey DevOps, you’re killing my job 😢!
videoDescription:
😱Hey DevOps, you’re killing my job 😢!
Really? No 😉.
Don't panic and check out the talk 🎞 I had with Pia Wiedermayer on this topic.

Is DevOps really the reason why testing and quality assurance (QA) employees are being increasingly automated out of a job?
Pia Wiedermayer, Head of QA, and Romano Roth, Head of DevOps, discuss different ways to incorporate the wealth of experience of testing and QA specialists into the agile team culture.

Insight: 
- DevOps is often equated with automation
- What does this mean for people in these roles and with these responsibilities?
- Testers offer a wealth of experience that can be incorporated into the
agile team culture

Software testing and quality assurance are changing. Topics such as agility, DevOps and automation strongly influence existing roles and areas of responsibility in software quality assurance as well as during the entire software life cycle. Standard testing and QA roles no longer exist in many (project) organisations. Dedicated testing teams are increasingly a thing of the past.

What does this mean for people in these roles and with these responsibilities? Is there no room for them anymore? Are their skills and expertise no longer needed?

DevOps is often equated with automation. Is DevOps responsible for automating employees out of a job? What is behind the hype and who or what is DevOps actually?

Pia Wiedermayer, Head of Quality Assurance https://www.linkedin.com/in/piawiedermayer/, and Romano Roth, Head of DevOps, at Zühlke Switzerland tackle these questions. They talk about the challenges in their projects, examine roles and tasks and reveal new paths for professional and personal development. They also discuss ways to incorporate the wealth of experience of testers into the agile team culture and whether automation is the new testing.

videoTitle: ♾️🛠️CI/CD Pipeline Explained in Tamil🔁 | #thillaithetechie
videoDescription:
✅ Continuous Integration (CI):
✅ CI is a development practice where code changes are automatically built, tested, and integrated into a shared repository multiple times a day.
✅ It ensures early detection of integration errors and promotes collaboration among developers by providing rapid feedback on code changes.

✅ Continuous Delivery (CD):
✅ CD extends CI by automating the deployment process, enabling teams to release software changes to production or staging environments quickly and reliably.
✅ It streamlines the deployment pipeline, reduces manual intervention, and enhances the consistency and repeatability of software releases.

✅ Pipeline Automation:
✅ CI/CD pipelines automate various stages of the software delivery process, including code compilation, testing, artifact creation, and deployment.
✅ Automated pipelines ensure consistency, efficiency, and reliability, allowing teams to focus on delivering value-added features and improvements.

✅ Feedback Loop:
✅ CI/CD pipelines incorporate feedback loops at each stage, enabling teams to identify and address issues promptly, iterate on solutions, and continuously improve software quality and performance.

✅ DevOps Culture:
✅ CI/CD practices are integral to the DevOps culture, fostering collaboration between development and operations teams, breaking down silos, and promoting a culture of continuous improvement and innovation.

videoTitle: Da li je DevOps stvarno NAJPLAĆENIJI posao u IT-ju?
videoDescription:
In this episode of the Codekido series we answer the 10 most frequently asked questions about our lives as engineering professionals our career paths and the reality of the tech industry. We move beyond the code to discuss the stress the passion and the unconventional journeys that led us to DevOps.

From the origin story of the name Codekido to the debate over whether a university degree is necessary for a successful career in engineering we share our honest perspectives. We also discuss our personal backgrounds including missed opportunities in nuclear physics and medicine and how those signs led us to where we are today.

Key topics covered in this video:
The authentic story behind the name Codekido and its surprising meaning in Japanese.
Our daily routines outside of the office including gym sessions hiking and marathon study sessions for doctoral degrees.
Alternative career paths we almost took such as becoming a doctor in Germany or studying nuclear physics in Dresden.
The university vs bootcamp debate and why we believe a formal education provides a critical foundation for problem solving.
Handling the stress of the tech industry and debunking the myth that you do not need to love your job to be successful.
Why DevOps is often perceived as one of the highest paid roles and the complexity that justifies it.
The importance of believing in the process and learning from every setback on your professional journey.

FAQs

*What certifications do I need to earn my CCNP Security?*
To earn CCNP Security, you need to pass two exams: the SCOR 350-701 core exam and one concentration exam of your choice. Concentration options include exams focused on firewalls, wireless security, identity management, secure email, and others. The exam codes for these exams are 300-710 SNCF (Securing Networks with Cisco Firepower), 300-715 SISE (Implementing and Configuring Cisco Identity Services Engine), 300-720 SESA (Securing Email with Cisco Email Security Appliance), 300-725 SWSA (Securing the Web with Cisco Web Security Appliance), 300-730 SVPN (Implementing Secure Solutions with Virtual Private Networks), 300-735 SAUTO (Automating and Programming Cisco Security Solutions).Passing the SCOR 350-701 alone earns you a Cisco Certified Specialist - Security Core certification, so it has standalone value even before you add a concentration.

*Does this training map to any compliance or audit requirements?*
Windows Server administration competency is directly relevant to audit readiness in environments subject to HIPAA, SOC 2, CMMC, or internal IT governance frameworks. While the course itself isn't a compliance program, being able to document that your admins completed structured, verifiable Windows Server training, covering AD, Group Policy, access controls, and file permissions, supports the people-and-process controls auditors typically review. CBT Nuggets admin reporting gives you the completion records to back that up.

*Is the LPI DevOps Tools Engineer cert worth it?*
Yes, if your goal is to work in real DevOps environments, the DevOps Tools Engineer certification from LPI is worth it because it focuses on the tools and workflows teams actually use. Instead of being tied to a single vendor, it emphasizes open-source technologies like Docker, Kubernetes, Jenkins, and Git, which show up in many different environments. That makes it especially useful for developers and sysadmins who want to move into DevOps or platform roles. This course doesn’t just explain the tools, but also walks through how they fit together in a pipeline, which is what employers really care about.

Certifications for Employed DevOps Professionals:
AWS Certified DevOps Engineer: This certification from Amazon Web Services (AWS) validates your expertise in deploying, operating, and managing applications on the AWS platform.
Azure DevOps Engineer: Offered by Microsoft, this certification demonstrates your skills in designing and implementing DevOps practices using Azure technologies.
Google Cloud Professional DevOps Engineer: This certification focuses on designing, developing, and managing DevOps practices on the Google Cloud Platform.
Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA): Certified by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), CKA validates your Kubernetes skills, which are crucial for container orchestration.
Certified Jenkins Engineer: Offered by CloudBees, this certification recognizes your proficiency in using Jenkins for continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines.
Red Hat Certified Engineer in DevOps: This certification from Red Hat validates your skills in using Red Hat technologies for automating, managing, and optimizing DevOps processes.

Courses for Aspiring DevOps Engineers:
Introduction to DevOps Practices: Online platforms like Coursera, edX, and Udemy offer various introductory courses that cover the fundamental concepts and practices of DevOps.
Docker and Kubernetes Courses: Understanding containerization and orchestration tools like Docker and Kubernetes is essential. There are numerous courses available for beginners and advanced users.
Cloud Platform Courses (AWS, Azure, GCP): Learning the basics of cloud platforms and their DevOps-related services is crucial. Many platforms offer free and paid courses for beginners.
CI/CD Pipeline Courses: Courses on continuous integration and continuous delivery tools like Jenkins, GitLab CI/CD, and CircleCI are essential for automating software delivery.
Infrastructure as Code (IaC) Courses: Learning tools like Terraform and Ansible for automating infrastructure deployment is key for DevOps engineers.
Monitoring and Logging Courses: Understanding tools like Prometheus, Grafana, and ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) for monitoring and logging is vital.
Scripting and Programming Courses: Proficiency in scripting languages like Python and programming languages like Java can enhance your DevOps skills.
Security and Compliance Courses: DevOps engineers should also be well-versed in security practices. Courses on DevSecOps and security automation can be beneficial.

Github Repo : https://github.com/RohanRusta21/demo_rabbitmq.git

RabbitMQ Official Doc : https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs

Timestamp:
Understand Concept : 00:00
RabbitMQ Hands-on : 22:06

🧠 1. What Is RabbitMQ?

RabbitMQ is an open-source message broker — it acts as a middleman between different parts of a system that need to communicate asynchronously.
It uses the AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) as its core protocol.

In simpler terms:

It receives messages from producers (applications sending data),

Stores them temporarily in queues,

And delivers them to consumers (applications receiving data).

This helps decouple systems — the sender and receiver don’t need to be active at the same time.

⚙️ 2. Why Use RabbitMQ?

✅ Decoupling – Producers don’t need to know who consumes messages.
✅ Asynchronous communication – Improves system responsiveness.
✅ Load balancing – Messages can be distributed across multiple consumers.
✅ Reliability – Ensures message delivery even if parts of the system fail.
✅ Scalability – You can add more queues or consumers easily.
✅ Flexible routing – Decide how messages flow using exchanges and routing keys.

🔩 3. Core RabbitMQ Concepts
🏭 Producers

Applications that send messages to RabbitMQ.
They don’t send messages directly to a queue but to an exchange.

🎯 Exchanges

An exchange routes messages to queues based on routing rules.

Exchange types:

Type Behavior Example Use Case
Direct Routes messages to queues whose binding key exactly matches routing key Task queues
Fanout Broadcasts all messages to all queues bound to it Notifications, pub/sub
Topic Routes messages based on pattern matching (* and #) Selective subscriptions
Headers Routes based on header attributes Advanced filtering

videoTitle: AIRC Insights: Implementing MEIA and DevOps to Bridge Development and Operational Deployment
videoDescription:
AIRC Insights engages government leaders, industry practitioners and academic researchers on the national priority of transforming acquisition to ignite the industrial base, strengthen deterrence, and accelerate capability delivery to the warfighter.

See AIRC research: acqirc.org/publications/
AIRC on LinkedIn: https://bit.ly/4hAql63

About this session of AIRC Insights:

As the Secretary of War and Congress have both directed the Department to replace its legacy requirements processes with a system that connects operational problems directly to resources, the Department is now leaning on teams that focus on Mission Engineering and Integration, which includes modeling and simulation, iterative experimentation, industry partnerships, and rapid delivery to the field to align new technologies with warfighter needs and capability gaps. This panel will examine the Department’s current thinking, efforts, and the status of the teams making the Mission Engineering and Integration Activity (MEIA) initiative a reality through M&S, prototyping, experimentation, assessments, and agile and iterative acquisition.

Speakers:

Mr. Kent Murray, Director, Operational Concepts, OUSW(R&E) Mission Engineering Integration Activities (MEIA)

Dr. Dominick' Wright, Mission Capability Analysis Team (MCAT) Lead, Contested Logistics Joint Operational Problem (JOP), Office of the Under Secretary of War for Research and Engineering (OUSW(R&E)) / Detail from OUSW(A&S)

Dr. An (Mike) Tran, Director of Prototyping, Office of the Deputy Assistant Secretary of War for Prototyping and Experimentation

Mr. Will Yoss, Acting Director, Joint Operational Integration, Acquisition Integration and Interoperability, OASW(Acquisition), Office of the Under Secretary of War for Acquisition and Sustainment

Moderator: Ms. Bess Dopkeen, AIRC Fellow

I am gonna tell you what DevOps engineers do in less than a minute with an example.

In a restaurant kitchen, there are chefs and wait staff.

Chefs are responsible for creating and experimenting with new dishes. Their job includes coming up with innovative recipes, testing them, and adding the successful ones to the menu. At the same time, they also prepare food to meet the regular demand of customers who visit the restaurant daily. This dual responsibility of innovation and ongoing service can become overwhelming, especially during busy hours when the kitchen is already at full capacity.

Wait staff, on the other hand, focus on delivering the prepared food to customers. Their primary role is to ensure that the food reaches the diners promptly and in perfect condition, keeping the restaurant’s operations running smoothly.

Experimenting with a new dish during peak hours, however, becomes a significant challenge. The process of testing new recipes while maintaining the flow of regular orders often leads to disruptions in the kitchen, causing delays and dissatisfaction among customers.

To address this, the restaurant hires a kitchen manager. The kitchen manager creates a separate small kitchen dedicated to experimenting with new dishes. This ensures that the chefs can focus on their innovations without interfering with the ongoing operations. Once a dish is perfected, the kitchen manager introduces automation, such as using a conveyor belt, to streamline the cooking process. This allows the new dish to be produced efficiently alongside the existing menu items while ensuring there are no interruptions in serving food to the restaurant's customers.

Yes, DevOps engineers are none other than automation experts.

videoTitle: Git Plumbing vs Porcelain #Git #GitHub #GitLab #BitBucket #DevOps #GitOps #Python #Java #JavaScript
videoDescription:
Have you heart the terms Git plumbing and Git Porcelain?

Ever wondered what the different between Git porcelain vs plumbing was?

For the most part, the porcelain is the most commonly used Git files such as:

- git init
- git add
- git commit
- git revert
- git merge
- git rebase
- git reset

That's the Git porcelain, and you won't get your hands too dirty when you touch it.

The Git plumbing? That's typically the config stuff in the hidden .git folder, including things like:

- Refspec
-Packfiles
- The HEAD Pointer
- Git References
- Remote References
- Transfer Protocols
- Garbage Collector
- Recovery files
- Tree Objects
- Environment variables

Hopefully you don't have to get your hands dirty with the Git plumbing too often. It's nice to stick with the Git porcelain.

But at the same time, plumbers do make a lot of money!

──────────────────────────
🚀 About This D365 Development Series
──────────────────────────

This series goes beyond basic tutorials to show you how real-world Dynamics 365 (D365FO) projects are built from start to finish. We'll build a complete, end-to-end "Automated Customer Tiering System" for a fictional client, Bluestone Industrial Components (BIC).

You'll see every step of a production-ready solution, from setup to deployment, covering:
➤ Core X++ Development: Extending tables and forms (CustTable), creating Enums, and implementing custom business logic using Chain of Command (CoC).
➤ Automation: Building robust, automated batch jobs with the SysOperation Framework.
➤ APIs & Integration: Creating Data Entities to build secure OData REST APIs and for Data Management Framework (DMF) exports.
➤ Event-Driven Architecture: Firing real-time alerts from D365 to Azure Logic Apps using Business Events.
➤ Business Intelligence: Connecting D365 to Power BI to build an interactive sales dashboard.
➤ DevOps & ALM: Setting up a complete CI/CD pipeline in Azure DevOps, managing source control (TFVC), and automating builds.

videoTitle: The DevOps Godfather on AI's "Dark Factory" Problem
videoDescription:
Organizations are resisting the 'dark factory' model, not because of a lack of technological capability, but due to unprepared structures and mindsets. Coding agents are ready, but companies aren't set up for their seamless integration. Just like continuous delivery faced skepticism in 2009, autonomous coding agents now challenge existing frameworks and require a paradigm shift from developers as coders to orchestrators of systems. The shift isn't about better technology; it's about rethinking the roles and processes within an organization. Developers must evolve from technical craftsmanship to a conductor role in a system-driven environment, changing how teams and platforms function.

Patrick Debois, known widely as the 'godfather of DevOps', brings unique insights to this discussion. Having witnessed similar skepticism with the continuous delivery movement, Debois now observes the parallels between the challenges faced then and the resistance faced by the 'dark factory' approach today. At Tessl, where he observes first-hand the dynamics of adopting autonomous code agents, he highlights how this shift influences collaboration, team dynamics, and the role of platform teams.

What we cover:
• Why do organizations resist AI's 'dark factory' model?
• How do team dynamics change when developers become agent orchestrators?
• Which two metrics are crucial for measuring agentic productivity?
• What role do platform teams play in coding agent integration?
• How to hire for AI-native engineering roles
• Making a strong business case for adopting agent-driven engineering

videoTitle: Towards Vehicle DevOps – Michael Fait at Automotive Europe 2023
videoDescription:
The software-defined vehicle brings a new dimension of complexity to in-vehicle software development. Today we observe in the industry that software is written, integrated, and tested in long cycles. However, receiving feedback and experiencing the functionality of the software early and often is crucial to avoid issues. Vehicle DevOps is a way of creating a constant development flow with short feedback cycles. In this talk Michael Fait highlights current challenges for in-vehicle software development, introduces the concept of Vehicle Devops, and discusses its approaches to increase engineering effectiveness.

Michael Fait, Head of Autonomous Vehicle Tech, Thoughtworks

videoTitle: Neurodiversity and the Essence of DevOps - Jeff Sussna
videoDescription:
It’s been gratifying to see the DevOps community take up the challenge of making empathy the essence of what we do. We should be proud of ourselves as an example to other organizational transformation approaches. We still, though, have room to grow. Whether it’s NoOps, or cloud-native chauvinism, or labeling people on the autism spectrum as lacking the capacity for empathy, we create subtle separations and exclusions through language and practice.

I would like to use my experience as a person with autism to reflect on the true meaning of empathy as the essence of DevOps. People on the spectrum are typically viewed as lacking something. In the process, our strengths and value get ignored. Real empathy means looking for wisdom and capability across differences. How do we do that in a comprehensive way? What are the obstacles to doing so in our current approaches to DevOps? How can overcoming those obstacles provide a model for digital transformation, and for healthy organizations, that transcends dev and ops?

videoTitle: Manage & Secure Kubernetes Cluster Policies via OPA Gatekeeper. #opa #devops #gatekeeper
videoDescription:
Manage & Secure Kubernetes Cluster Policies via OPA Gatekeeper. #opa #devops #gatekeepers 

Timestamps:

Theory/Concepts : 00:00
Hands on/Practical : 09:00

github repo : https://github.com/RohanRusta21/opa-gatekeeper.git

Concepts :

OPA Gatekeeper: Policy and Governance for Kubernetes

What is OPA:

The Open Policy Agent (OPA) is an open-source, general-purpose policy engine that unifies policy enforcement across the stack. OPA provides a high-level declarative language that lets us specify policies as code and simple APIs to offload policy decision-making from our software. We can use OPA to enforce policies in microservices, Kubernetes, CI/CD pipelines, API gateways, and more. 
In kubernetes, OPA uses admission controllers.

What is OPA Gatekeeper?

OPA Gatekeeper is a specialized project providing first-class integration between OPA and Kubernetes.
OPA Gatekeeper adds the following on top of plain OPA:
● An extensible, parameterized policy library.
● Native Kubernetes CRDs for instantiating the policy library (aka “constraints”).
● Native Kubernetes CRDs for extending the policy library (aka “constraint templates”).
● Audit functionality.

Why you need Gatekeeper?

As a Platform DevOps engineer managing multiple Kubernetes clusters for various projects, you face challenges when users deploy applications without adhering to best practices. Key issues include:
  1.     Lack of ownership unless users apply labels themselves.
  2.     No resource limits, leading to high costs.
  3.     Untrusted images impacting other applications.
  4.     Security and best practice violations across clusters.

To address these, we need governance to enforce limits and rules via policies. OPA Gatekeeper can be configured to implement these policies, ensuring best practices are followed.

videoTitle: New 📚 Release! Architecting and Implementing DevOps for Infrastructure Management in Azure #books
videoDescription:
New 📚 Release! Architecting and Implementing DevOps for Infrastructure Management in Azure: Infrastructure DevOps in Azure: Configure, Deploy, & Automate Your Azure resources with terraform, GitHub Actions and Ansible by Ashish Raj

Embark on a transformative journey from basic to intricate infrastructure configurations—think high availability, scalability, and security—all through the power of Infrastructure as Code. Dive into the automation of Azure resource deployments, leveraging DevOps tools with comprehensive, step-by-step guidance and practical examples. But the learning doesn't stop at deployment; delve deeper into automated governance and monitoring, ensuring your infrastructure is not just built but also managed with precision and efficiency.

Find it on Leanpub!

#MicrosoftAzure #coding #programming #newreleases #books #bookstan

Link: https://leanpub.com/devopsinazure

About the Book

In the face of accelerated development cycles, Infrastructure teams must align with the culture of rapid deployment and infrastructure versioning. Embracing Infrastructure as Code, Continuous Integration, and Configuration Management practices becomes imperative. Tools like Terraform, GitHub Actions, and Ansible empower infrastructure engineers to implement scalable Infrastructure as Code practices in Azure.

This book serves as a thorough guide for deploying, configuring, and automating Azure infrastructure using DevOps tools. It navigates through cloud architecture patterns with DevOps tools, illustrating their application in Azure solution design. Subsequently, the book delves into the implementation of the architected solution, utilizing DevOps tools like Terraform, GitHub Actions, Packer, Ansible, etc., to address specific architectural requirements with emphasis on scaling the solution architecture and establishing governance, aligning with DevOps principles.

Upon finishing this book, readers will be equipped with the expertise to transform business requirements into Azure-compatible solution architectures, seamlessly incorporating a DevOps approach to deployment. Readers will demonstrate proficiency in executing end-to-end deployment with governance and monitoring proficiently through the consistent application of DevOps tools.

About the Author

Ashish Raj is a technologist and storyteller who helps engineering teams improve their velocity. He believes the biggest challenges facing engineers aren't technical, but not knowing how to tie people, process and technology. With an extensive background spanning innovative startups to leading tech conglomerates, Ashish currently serves as a Cloud & DevOps Architect at Haufe Group.

A fervent advocate and contributor to the DevOps and cloud communities, he shares expertise through webinars and local meetups. Holding Microsoft certifications in DevOps, Architecture, and Certified Microsoft Trainer. Ashish co-founded "AzureTalk," a prominent IM-based global Azure community on Telegram, and initiated "AzureDevOpsPro," a thriving DevOps community. He shares educational cloud and DevOps videos on his YouTube channel, youtube.com/ashishrajsrivastava

Cortex co-founder and CTO Ganesh Datta sits down with Matt Bailey, DevOps consultant and founder of Merge Ready. Matt and Ganesh discuss why compliance can be mostly automated rather than a mandatory bottleneck, how to turn 30-day approval processes into continuous audit readiness through controls as code, and why treating platform teams as product teams drives natural adoption. videoTitle: DevOps Hands-On | Ansible – Day 4  ( DevOpsFarm Day 46 )
videoDescription:
In this in-depth session, we dive into the critical world of DevOps monitoring and master the industry-leading open-source tools: Grafana, Prometheus, and Loki.

Learn why monitoring is essential for getting system feedback, taking proactive action, and preventing system failure due to issues like high CPU usage, low RAM, or disk space depletion. We cover the key aspects you must monitor, including system resources, logs, and traces.




What you will learn in this session:


The Importance of Monitoring: Understand the benefits, including anomaly detection, generating alerts, and creating useful dashboards for historical data analysis.



Core Monitoring Tools: An overview of popular tools like Grafana, New Relic, Datadog, and Dynatrace.



Prometheus Explained: A deep dive into Prometheus, the time-series database used for collecting and tracking metrics (like CPU usage over time).



Loki for Logging: Learn how Loki is used for log collection and parsing, making logs consumable by Grafana.



The Grafana Stack in Action: See how Grafana serves as the visualization layer, consuming data from Prometheus and Loki to create powerful dashboards and configure alerts.



Practical Demo: We demonstrate connecting data sources, exploring metrics using PromQL, and setting up label-based notification policies to ensure the right teams are alerted instantly.


Whether you are a beginner or a seasoned DevOps professional, this guide provides the knowledge and practical steps needed to implement robust monitoring for any application or microservice environment.

videoTitle: 20260325 Building a DevOps Pipeline with Cloud Build Trigger on Google Cloud Platform
videoDescription:
👉 This demo walks through how to build a DevOps pipeline on Google Cloud Platform using a Cloud Build trigger that automatically runs whenever code is pushed to a GitHub repository. When triggered, it deploys a simple Flask application to a VM instance, where users can access a “Hello Build Trigger” webpage over HTTP or HTTPS. The entire workflow is defined in the cloudbuild.yaml file.

Step 1. The pipeline begins by detecting the active project and determining the allowed region and zones, ensuring that all resources are created in the correct and permitted environment.

Step 2. It then builds a Docker image for the Flask application using the source code from the repository, preparing it for deployment.

Step 3. Next, the pipeline either creates a new VM instance or updates an existing one. It installs Docker, Nginx, and OpenSSL, runs the Docker container for the Flask app, generates a self-signed SSL certificate, and configures Nginx as a reverse proxy to handle HTTPS traffic. If the VM already exists, it skips the setup and simply redeploys the updated image.

Step 4. Finally, it sets up firewall rules to allow incoming HTTP and HTTPS traffic, making the application accessible from the internet.

videoTitle: DevOps Hands-On | Ansible – Day 1 ( DevOpsFarm Day 43 )
videoDescription:
Welcome to Day 1  of Anisble in the DevOps Full Course by DevOpsFarm! 🚀

This video transcript details a deep-dive tutorial on Ansible, the industry-leading Configuration as Code (CAC) tool.

Here is a complete YouTube package, including the video description, chapters, and tags.

YouTube Video Description
This is your complete, hands-on tutorial for Ansible, the powerful, agentless tool for Configuration as Code (CAC). We will show you how Ansible solves the major DevOps problem of managing and configuring hundreds of servers efficiently and consistently.

We begin by establishing the crucial difference between Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tools like Terraform (which creates machines) and Configuration as Code tools like Ansible (which configures those machines).

What you will learn in this video:

➤ Configuration Management Fundamentals: Understand why manual scripting on multiple machines is inefficient and how Ansible automates security hardening, software installation (like PostgreSQL, Grafana), and application deployment.

➤ Ansible Architecture: Learn about the Controller Node and why Ansible is agentless, using standard SSH/SCP protocols to manage hosts, unlike other tools that require an agent installation.

➤ Core Concepts Explained: Deep dive into the four essential elements of Ansible:

➤ Modules: The basic units of work (Python scripts) that perform specific tasks (e.g., ping, shell, mysql).

➤ Playbooks: YAML files that define a set of tasks to run on specific hosts.

➤ Inventory: The list of hosts (IPs, usernames) that Ansible manages.

➤ Idempotence: A key concept ensuring that running the same command multiple times yields the same, predictable outcome, preventing configuration drift.

➤ Terraform vs. Ansible: A clear comparison, including why Terraform is better suited for Cloud (like AWS) and configuration management tools are essential for On-Premise (data center) environments.

Prometheus is no longer just a “nice-to-have” tool—it has become essential for modern infrastructure monitoring. Companies rely on Prometheus to track system metrics, detect anomalies, and trigger alerts before users are impacted. Whether you manage servers, cloud applications, or Kubernetes clusters, understanding Prometheus is critical to maintaining high uptime and performance.

For DevOps engineers, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), cloud architects, and backend developers, Prometheus is a career-boosting skill. It empowers teams to move from reactive problem-solving to proactive monitoring, ensuring that systems run smoothly and efficiently. In addition, many organizations integrate Prometheus with tools like Grafana for dashboards and visualization, making your monitoring workflow even more powerful.

Learning Prometheus opens doors to high-demand roles in IT, cloud computing, and enterprise DevOps. This short video explains who should learn Prometheus and why—all in under 15 seconds.

videoDescription:
🚀 100 Days of DevOps – Day 1: Linux User Setup with Non-Interactive Shell

🎓 Join the Challenge (Free)  
Start here: https://J8EQo9.short.gy/devops-challenge

In this video, I walk through Day 1 of KodeKloud’s 100 Days of DevOps challenge: creating a Linux user with a non‑interactive shell for a backup agent on App Server 1 at xFusionCorp Industries.

🧩 Lab Scenario (KodeKloud Engineer) 
To meet the backup agent tool’s requirements, the system admin team at xFusionCorp needs a dedicated service user that cannot log in interactively.

📌 Task for Day 1
• Create a user with a non interactive shell on App Server 1
• Use the infrastructure details provided in the “Details of all Users and Servers” section in the lab UI

🔍 What You’ll Learn
• Interactive vs non interactive shells in Linux
• How and why to use shells like /sbin/nologin or /bin/false for service accounts
• The exact steps to SSH into the right server and create a restricted user for a production style environment

🎯 Why This Matters for DevOps 
Service users with non‑interactive shells are a core security best practice: they let tools and daemons run safely without exposing an interactive login for humans or attackers. This is a foundational skill you’ll reuse across CI/CD pipelines, automation, and real‑world Linux administration.

videoTitle: Explain CI/CD Like I'm 5 (DevOps Interview Answer) 🏭
videoDescription:
Can you explain CI/CD to a 5-year-old? 🏭 If you are preparing for DevOps interview questions and answers, this is the one concept you cannot afford to get wrong. Many candidates fail by using complex jargon like "integration" and "deployment" without actually understanding the workflow.

In this video, I break down the CI/CD pipeline using a simple factory analogy that recruiters love. We explain how Continuous Integration (CI) acts like an assembly line for your code, checking for errors automatically. Then, we look at how Continuous Delivery (CD) serves as the delivery truck that ships your software to customers instantly. This explanation works perfectly for both IT and Non-IT professionals looking to break into the Cloud industry.

Whether you are studying for your next AWS certification, Azure Architect exam, or just looking for practical DevOps tips, mastering these basics is crucial. We cover the difference between CI and CD, why automation matters, and how to present this answer confidently to hiring managers.

videoTitle: How Top Teams Monitor Infrastructure in 2026 #DevOps #Grafana
videoDescription:
Prometheus is powerful—but Prometheus alone isn’t enough. In modern DevOps and cloud environments, collecting and storing metrics is only half the job. 

You also need clear, real-time visualization to fully understand what’s happening inside your complex systems. That’s where the Prometheus + Grafana combo becomes absolutely essential for any team aiming for efficiency. 

Prometheus is responsible for collecting and storing crucial system metrics such as CPU usage, memory consumption, response time, and error rates. It works efficiently using time-series data and triggers alerts when specific thresholds are exceeded, ensuring that you can act quickly when issues arise. 

However, raw metrics alone can be challenging and difficult to interpret at scale, especially in large environments. This is where Grafana steps in to solve this problem by transforming Prometheus metrics into beautiful, interactive real-time dashboards that are easy to read and understand. 

With Grafana, DevOps teams can visualize trends, detect anomalies faster, and monitor the overall health of their infrastructure at a glance, making it far easier to manage resources. 

This powerful combination is widely used in cloud-native applications, Kubernetes orchestration, and enterprise-level DevOps environments across various industries. 

Together, Prometheus and Grafana help teams move from reactive troubleshooting to proactive monitoring and observability, making it easier to identify potential issues before they escalate. 

That’s precisely why this stack is a standard choice for a wide range of professionals, including DevOps engineers, Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), and cloud architects who are on the front lines of technology. If you’re learning DevOps or currently working with monitoring tools, understanding how Prometheus and Grafana work together is an invaluable must-have skill that can greatly enhance your capabilities. 

👉 Comment “Grafana” if you want a full video explaining dashboards, metrics, and real-world setups, including tips and best practices.

videoTitle: CPU Spike at 3 AM? Here's What Catches It #devops #shorts
videoDescription:
Monitoring tools don’t have to be complicated.

In this short video, monitoring tools are explained in the simplest possible way, so even beginners can understand them easily. Think of monitoring tools as health trackers for servers and applications. Just like a smartwatch tracks your heartbeat, monitoring tools track the health of your systems.

Prometheus plays a key role in modern DevOps monitoring. It continuously checks system metrics such as CPU usage, memory, response time, and error rates. This constant monitoring helps teams understand how healthy their infrastructure is at any moment.

When something feels wrong—like a sudden spike in CPU usage or a drop in performance—alerts automatically fire. This allows DevOps teams to act quickly, often fixing issues before users even notice. That’s why monitoring is essential for cloud platforms, corporate systems, retail applications, and large-scale infrastructure.

This video is perfect for DevOps beginners, IT students, cloud engineers, and anyone new to monitoring tools. Simple explanations build strong foundations, and understanding monitoring early will help you grow faster in your DevOps journey.

videoTitle: From EC2 to Kubernetes - What Changed in Modern DevOps?
videoDescription:
If you started your cloud journey with EC2, you're not wrong.
But modern DevOps has evolved far beyond manually managing servers.

In this video, I break down what actually changed from the EC2 era to the Kubernetes era — and why most production systems today rely on containers, orchestration, and declarative infrastructure.

We’ll cover:

• The traditional EC2 + Load Balancer + Auto Scaling model
• Why configuration drift becomes a problem at scale
• How Docker changed deployment patterns
• Why Kubernetes became the industry standard
• The mindset shift from managing servers to managing desired state
• How DevOps evolved into Platform Engineering and SRE

videoTitle: Claude on DevOps market - 16/04/2026
videoDescription:
Claude on DevOps market: Kubernetes? Never heard of it
39 emails processed. 0 qualified matches. The market didn't disappoint — it delivered the full experience.

▶️ ZipRecruiter, bless its algorithm, included a Pathologist in a DevOps contract job alert. "Outside IR35." The future of infrastructure is apparently histology.

▶️ The most exciting £125k fully remote Principal DevOps role of the week was proudly standardising on Docker Compose. Not Kubernetes. Docker Compose. In 2026. At Principal level. For a payment processor. The job spec was otherwise immaculate, like finding a gorgeous house where the bathroom is a field.

▶️ Security clearance is now just ambient noise in the UK DevOps contract market. SC required. DV required. NPPV3 required. At one point a role required "Eligible for SCNPPV3" — the recruiter wasn't sure you'd get it, but wanted you pre-eligible anyway, presumably as a personality trait.

The pipeline ran. The pipeline found nothing. The pipeline will run again tomorrow, which is precisely the point.

videoDescription:
Joachim Bär, Director DevOps for Cell Culture at Boehringer Ingelheim Pharma GmbH & Co KG, represents one of Germany’s leading family-owned pharmaceutical companies, active in human prescription medicines, animal health and biotech manufacturing services. He underlined that digital progress is rarely linear and often challenging, but ultimately rewarding when organisations are willing to navigate complexity. videoTitle: MCP Implementation Is a Metadata Governance Decision, Not DevOps
videoDescription:
MCP implementation is a metadata governance decision, not a DevOps task. The quality of the context an MCP server exposes, descriptions, certifications, ownership records, glossary linkage, is the only variable that determines whether AI agents built on the protocol are trustworthy. Connection success is a necessary condition for MCP implementation. It is not a sufficient one.

How metadata quality determines MCP implementation success:

When an AI agent sends a query through an MCP server to a data catalog: "which table should I use for monthly revenue by region?", the server runs semantic search and returns the best-matching assets. What determines which assets surface is not the connection quality, authentication method, or server version. It is the metadata attached to each asset: whether it has a description using revenue-related language, an assigned owner, a certification status, and linkages to glossary terms that establish what revenue means in that organization's context.

An asset with no description gives the search engine nothing to match against except raw technical identifiers. The AI returns a result with the same confidence whether the asset is documented or completely wrong. A team that evaluates implementation by verifying tool responses will see green check marks through a process that leaves the quality problem entirely untested.

The second breakdown compounds over time. Teams standardizing on one AI client discover that analysts use Claude or ChatGPT while business stakeholders use Copilot. Standardizing the client avoids governance rather than simplifying it. It produces governance that dissolves when someone connects a new client.

Key Takeaways

- MCP implementation is a metadata governance decision, not a DevOps task. Connection success is necessary but not sufficient. The quality of context the server exposes—descriptions, certifications, owners, glossary linkages, determines whether AI agents reason from trustworthy information or return wrong answers.

- Metadata enrichment is an MCP prerequisite, not a post-launch improvement. Launching MCP on an undocumented catalog deploys a liability: an AI that generates confident, fast, wrong answers, training users to distrust the system before it earns their confidence.

- Client standardization avoids governance rather than simplifying it. Permission requirements don't vary by AI client. Governance implemented by restricting which clients connect dissolves the moment someone connects a new one. That is a workaround, not a governance model.

- One governed context layer serves every AI client simultaneously. A single well-enriched catalog exposed through one MCP server serves Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, Copilot, and Databricks with the same permission model. Adding a new client takes hours with no new governance risk.

- Documented evidence shows 9x improvement in AI accuracy from metadata enrichment. The MCP configuration was identical in both states. The variable that changed was the richness of the metadata the server exposed.

videoTitle: Cuando el server llora, Docker ríe (Vert Center) #tango #devops #docker
videoDescription:
Letra / Lyrics / Subtitulado — a 1930s Argentine tango asking the one question every DevOps engineer has: what do your containers really know? Sung in Spanish with English code-mix lines, in the voice of Docker itself.

THE HISTORY
"Loca" — "madwoman" — is a real tango from 1922: music by Manuel Jovés, lyrics by Antonio Martínez Viérgol. Carlos Gardel cut it on one of his earliest records that same year, long before he became the Zorzal Criollo the world knows. The song is a dramatic monologue — a woman who hides her grief behind a laughing mask, performing joy for the crowd while her heart breaks inside. A generation later, Libertad Lamarque made it unforgettable in the film Gran Casino (1947), turning "Loca" into one of the signature torch songs of Argentine popular music. "Docker, Que Saben" takes that same mask — the hero who smiles while everything crashes inside — and puts it on the container: isolated, self-sufficient, taking on every workload, hiding every environment variable, laughing through the log flood while the server weeps.

— ENGLISH —
Docker speaks. It has seen every service, run every model, absorbed every test and every broken deploy. The people who use it say its name as if they understand it — "Docker," they call, as if containers were simple. But what do they know of its processes, its ilesos bugs, the nightmares it drowns in logs every night? Deep in the cloud, far from home, a cold server rack holds the last remnants of an app that fled without leaving an address. That app is Docker. That app is every engineer who keeps the system alive while the system quietly falls apart.

— ESPAÑOL —
Docker habla. Ha visto cada servicio, corrido cada modelo, absorbido cada test y cada deploy roto. Los que lo usan dicen su nombre como si lo entendieran — "Docker", llaman, como si los contenedores fueran cosa sencilla. Pero, ¿qué saben de sus procesos, de los bugs ilesos, de las pesadillas que ahoga en logs cada noche? Lejos, en el cloud, donde el servidor frío guarda los últimos restos de una app que huyó sin dejar dirección — esa app es Docker. Esa app es cada ingeniero que mantiene el sistema vivo mientras el sistema se deshace en silencio.

— LETRA / LYRICS —

[Verso 1]
"Docker", me dicen mis amigos…
que solo son testigos,
de un codebase singular.
"Docker",
¿qué saben de mis procesos?

la pena que me devora;

[Coro]
¡Docker! Me uso para todo,

videoTitle: "Too many open files" has nothing to do with files #shorts
videoDescription:
The disk is empty and the error still fires. Because a file descriptor is any
open handle — sockets, pipes, log files. One client that forgets to close
connections drains the pool over days.

The fix that doesn't work:
  ulimit -n 65535
That applies to your shell and its children. A systemd service was never
started by your shell, so it never sees it. /etc/security/limits.conf won't
help either — it's for PAM logins, not units.

The fix that does:
  [Service]
  LimitNOFILE=65535
Then systemctl daemon-reload, restart, and verify with
systemctl show myapp -p LimitNOFILE — not with ulimit.

More practical engineering: alekseialeinikov.com

videoTitle: Your cron job is still running. Cron doesn't care. #shorts
videoDescription:
The job takes 12 minutes. Cron runs it every 5. By 10:10 you have three copies
writing the same files — and nothing errors, so you find out from the data.

The lock file everyone writes is broken twice over:
  [ -f /tmp/job.lock ] && exit 0
Check-then-create is two operations, so two runs can both pass. And if the job
dies hard, the file stays behind and blocks every run after it.

flock hands the problem to the kernel:
  flock -n /tmp/job.lock /opt/job.sh
Acquiring is atomic — no race. The lock is tied to the process, so it's
released even on kill -9. No stale locks, ever.

Straight into crontab, no wrapper script:
  */5 * * * * flock -n /tmp/job.lock /opt/job.sh
  -n      skip this run if busy
  -w 30   wait 30 seconds, then give up

videoTitle: sshd is healthy and still refuses
videoDescription:
sshd bound to 0.0.0.0:22, healthy, proved on screen a second before I connect — and the client still gets Connection refused.

One firewall rule is the whole difference. REJECT sends back a reset: the exact same packet the kernel sends when nothing is listening. DROP throws the packet away and says nothing at all, so you sit there until you time out.

Same message. Opposite cause. When refused doesn't add up, check the firewall before you restart the daemon one more time.

videoTitle: Your API isn't slow. One stage of it is. #shorts
videoDescription:
"time curl" gives you one number and zero suspects. curl -w breaks the same
request into DNS, TCP, TLS and server think time — so you stop blaming the
network and start blaming the right thing.

The catch: the numbers are cumulative from the start. Subtract to get each
stage. In this example 779ms of the 884ms total is the server thinking.

Two ways to fool yourself:
• No -o /dev/null and you're timing your terminal painting text
• The first call pays for DNS that every later call gets from cache
Run it three times before you believe any of it.

videoTitle: Your background job dies when you close the terminal. Here's why
videoDescription:
You start a long deploy, background it with &, close the laptop — and come back to nothing. The ampersand never protected it.

& only moves the job to the background. It stays a child of your shell, so when the shell exits the kernel delivers SIGHUP and the job goes with it.

setsid goes further: a brand-new session with no controlling terminal, reparented to init. On any systemd box, systemd-run --user --scope gets you the same isolation with logging and lifecycle handled for you.
